mcqs.question: Why can a chip with more cores but a weaker interconnect actually perform worse than one with fewer cores and a stronger interconnect?
options: Because more cores always draw more total power regardless of the interconnect
Because cores can only be as parallel as their ability to communicate, and contention on a weak communication fabric can become the bottleneck rather than raw compute capacity
Because operating systems can only schedule work on a limited number of cores
Because compilers cannot generate code for chips with many cores
mcqs.explanation: Parallel work generates coherence traffic, shared-cache access, and memory requests that all traverse the interconnect — if that fabric is contended, adding more cores doesn't help and can even hurt, since compute capacity was never the limiting factor. Power draw, OS scheduling limits, and compiler core-count limits aren't the mechanism described here.

mcqs.question: What is the main drawback of a crossbar interconnect that limits its use to smaller core counts?
options: It cannot support cache coherence protocols at all
Its area and power cost grow quadratically with the number of connected cores/ports, making it impractical well before core counts reach the dozens
It can only connect cores that are physically adjacent to each other
It has lower bandwidth than a shared bus
mcqs.explanation: A crossbar's any-to-any wiring requires roughly N² switching elements for N ports, so cost explodes quickly as core count grows, which is why it doesn't scale to many-core designs despite its excellent bandwidth. It can support coherence, isn't restricted to adjacent cores (that's a mesh characteristic), and has higher, not lower, bandwidth than a bus.

mcqs.question: Why do large-core-count chips typically adopt a mesh/Network-on-Chip topology instead of a bus or crossbar?
options: Mesh topologies have lower total bandwidth than a bus but are cheaper to manufacture
A mesh's cost grows roughly linearly with core count since each added core only needs local neighbor connections, unlike a bus's fixed shared bandwidth or a crossbar's quadratic wiring cost
Mesh topologies eliminate the need for any routing logic between cores
Buses and crossbars cannot be implemented on a single chip
mcqs.explanation: The mesh's local-connectivity-plus-routing design scales roughly linearly in cost as cores are added, avoiding both the bus's fixed-bandwidth contention and the crossbar's quadratic wiring blowup. Mesh bandwidth is generally higher than a contended bus, mesh networks require routers (routing logic) at every tile, and buses/crossbars are in fact implementable on-chip, just not scalable to large core counts.
